title: The calf and the second tablets (Exodus 32–34)
hookLine: the covenant breaks, the tablets shatter, new ones are carved; the Talmud says both were kept in the ark (Berakhot 8b)
carry: the broken tablets were kept too

cards: A drawer, a shoebox, a folder on a laptop: plenty of homes keep one, full of things that are broken but can't be thrown away. A cracked mug from a grandparent. A letter from a friendship that ended.
A cast from a broken arm. Moses has been up the mountain for forty days, and the people below decide he isn't coming back. What happens next breaks the covenant almost as soon as it's made.
And at the end of it, something broken ends up in the ark itself.

teach.b: The people panic and go to Aaron: make us a god to lead us. He collects their gold earrings, and a golden calf comes out of the fire. They bring offerings, eat, drink and dance.
On the mountain, God tells Moses what's happening. Moses comes down carrying two stone tablets, written, the Torah says, by the finger of God.
He sees the calf and the dancing, throws the tablets down, and they shatter at the foot of the mountain. It's a terrible scene, and the Torah doesn't soften it.
Then Moses goes back up and pleads for the people, and the story turns.

God reveals a description of divine mercy that synagogues still sing on fast days and holy days, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth."
And God says: "Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first." This time Moses carves the stones himself.

Jewish tradition says he came down with the second tablets on the tenth of Tishrei, the day that became Yom Kippur, the day of forgiveness. Now the Talmud's surprise. What happened to the broken pieces?
You'd expect them to be swept away. Instead, the Talmud teaches that the whole tablets and the broken tablets were placed together in the ark of the covenant.
And it draws a lesson: honor an elder who has forgotten their learning, because the broken tablets were kept in the ark too.

teach.h: HEW THEE TWO TABLES OF STONE.
teach.b: What broke is not thrown out. It travels with what was made new.

how: The Thirteen Attributes of Mercy from Exodus 34 are sung in synagogue on festivals, fast days and throughout Yom Kippur, which tradition links to the day the second tablets came down.

games.q: you're Moses. the tablets lie shattered at the foot of the mountain, and new ones have been carved. what do you do with the pieces?

put them in the ark with the new ones.
games.why: the Talmud says the whole tablets and the broken ones were kept together in the ark, and draws a lesson: honor the elder who has forgotten.

practice: Think of something broken in your life: an object, a friendship, a plan, a part of your health, a person who isn't who they used to be.
Don't fix it now; just give it a place, setting it down gently beside the things that are whole, in the same box. If a person came to mind, think of one way to honor them.

wordCard.voice: Shivrei luchot, Hebrew for the broken tablets: kept in the ark beside the new ones when the covenant was renewed.

orig.note: Hebrew: tablets. the shivrei luchot are the broken tablets.

carryVoice: Your line: the broken tablets were kept too. What broke still rides in the ark. See you tomorrow.
